newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economy slows down on lack of cash.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economy slows down on lack of cash.

text.p: Yugoslavia managed to retain relative macroeconomic stability in March but overall economic performance is slowing down and lack of cash remained a big problem, economists said on Wednesday.

"Basically, we have seen some stabilisation in prices, wages, pensions, consumption, industry output, but we cannot say for how long will this stabilisation last," Miroljub Labus, chief economist of the Economics Institute, told reporters.
Industry output slowed down somewhat and monthly inflation slightly picked up, the Belgrade-based institute said in its latest monthly report.
Macroeconomic stabilisation, even if temporary, could be a good start for reforms, Labus said.
"It can be a good basis to begin to restructure the economy, because it is always better to restructure under stable conditions." he said.
The economy experienced a 7.4 percent monthly industry growth and a moderate one percent inflation in March. This compares to 11.4 percent industry growth and a 0.6 percent February inflation.

Industries cited persistent lack of working capital as their biggest problem to increasing production, but economists were reluctant to support an idea of monetary relaxation which would create more funds for the capital-starved industry.
"With commercial banks penniless, the central bank has an alternative to finance the economy from its own sources but that leads to inflation," Labus said.
Instead of inflation, privatisation and other reforms, including changes in the companies' management, were seen as the only way for Yugoslavia to attract fresh foreign funds.
Labus played down some bankers' calls for a slight but highly controlled monetary relaxation.
"It is impossible to control money flows and extend credits to successful companies only. The central bank is not a commercial bank with credit potential for the economy.
"Besides, economic policy makers must take advantage of extreme illiquidity and let the economy restructure," he said.
Another economist with the institute, Goran Pitic, said banks and the state had an entirely different idea of how to keep money flows under control.

"We have experienced selective money flows. I am against any selective criteria in choosing successful firms to receive money. This economy is susceptible to any changes in money flows and to rising money supply. Without reforms, money ends up in the most unhealthy parts of the economy," Pitic said.

The central bank's tight money policy resulted in reduced share of cash in circulation in the M1 money supply to 45 from 54 percent at the end of February, which helped market prices stabilise, the Institute said.

Total M1 money supply at the end of February stood at 5.157 billion dinars ($917.63 million) and was 340 million lower than at the end of December. Cash in circulation fell by 620 million dinars to 2.336 billion dinars over the period.
But economists said there was plenty of room for further reduction of cash in circulation.
"Cash in circulation has been further cut down in March and April which helped the dinar black market rate strengthen in real terms to 3.5 to the German mark," Labus said.

Apart from tight monetary policy, macroeconomic stability in March was achieved after the government managed to overcome fiscal crisis, impose stricter financial discipline and collect more taxes than in February.

Due to a lack of financial discipline, the state collected in February only 2.58 billion dinars in taxes. In March it collected 3.8 billion dinars, compared to a record monthly 3.9 billion collected in December 1996, Labus said.

Despite some relaxation in the fiscal crisis, problems have remained and economists said Yugoslavia's GDP, estimated to grow to around 103 billion dinars in 1997, could not sustain public spending accounting for around 50 percent of its GDP. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
($1 = 5.6199 Yugoslav dinars)
